title: We’re building GoDotter, an open-source Cursor-like tool for Godot. Would love honest feedback!
author: feexthefox
selftext:
Hey everyone!

We’ve been building **GoDotter** for a while, an open-source AI assistant for Godot 4

The rough idea is: Cursor, but shaped around how Godot actually works. Scenes, nodes, scripts, logs, diffs, the editor itself. Not just a generic chatbot sitting next to your project

I want to be careful with the pitch because I know how people feel about AI tools. I feel the same way about a lot of them. I do not want more AI slop in games. I do not want a tool that pretends to make creative decisions for you

What I do want is something that helps with the annoying parts around the creative work

Things like:  
understanding a messy scene or script faster  
planning changes before touching files  
fixing GDScript or Godot errors from logs  
reviewing diffs before anything gets applied  
making small project edits without losing control  
helping newer Godot users learn what is going on instead of just guessing

It is still early. Some parts will be rough. That is part of why I am posting here instead of pretending it is finished

The project is open source and MIT licensed. You can inspect it, fork it, open issues, submit PRs, or just tell us what feels wrong

GitHub:  
[https://github.com/Lolner95/godotter](https://github.com/Lolner95/godotter)

The biggest thing I am looking for is real feedback from people actually making games in Godot

What would make this useful enough to keep open while working?  
What would make you immediately uninstall it?  
Where do AI tools usually get Godot wrong?  
What workflow should we support before anything else?

I would rather hear blunt feedback now than build the wrong thing quietly

Thanks to anyone who tries it, breaks it, reports something, or even just tells us the idea is bad in a useful way

comments.author: OneTwoThree231
comments.body:
The idea sounds good, but just wondering how this would differ from something like Codex?

Personally, I would have loved something like this some time ago when I was starting out with game dev :)

replies.author: feexthefox
replies.body:
That’s a fair question!

The main difference is that this would live directly inside Godot, so it can understand the project with more context than a general coding assistant. For example, when you run a scene with F5 or F6 and something breaks, it can already see the error logs, the scene structure, and the relevant Godot data instead of you having to copy everything over manually

I’m also trying to make it better at understanding more complex Godot-specific cases, especially 3D scenes. That’s where I’ve seen tools like Codex or Cursor struggle a lot. They can help with code, but they don’t really “see” the project the way Godot does

So the goal is not just another AI coding tool. I want it to feel native to Godot and actually useful for the problems game devs hit every day

And yeah, I had the same feeling. I would’ve loved something like this when I was starting out too 😛

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body:
How does the fact that it lives in the editor help it? Isn't all that information you mention available outside the editor through logs, the project assets, the LSP or even remote debugging?

Tools like Claude code have pretty advanced agentic tools at this point, it seems like we should be leveraging those.

replies.author: feexthefox
replies.body:
Yeah, fair point!

From my experience over the last 6 months using Cursor/Codex with Godot, the answers just get noticeably better when the tool is operating closer to the engine itself. I don’t have a perfect technical explanation for why, but it has been very clear in practice

Long term, the idea is to build very Godot-specific skills around 3D scenes, scripts, errors, project structure, etc., so it becomes more than just a generic agent pointed at files

That said, if Claude/Codex become good enough and this ends up making more sense as an MCP layer, I wouldn’t argue with that. The real goal is just making Godot development with AI less painful

replies.author: OneTwoThree231
replies.body:
I don't know if it's possible, but it might be nice to have something in Godot which can check through all the code you've written and make it the best and most optimised it can be to improve performance and reduce file size without me having to know. Like, I can just press a button to optimise and the plugin checks everything and all the nodes Godot has to improve it.

At the moment, I just put the best practices in my AGENTS file and that seems to be helping somewhat but going through so many files in codex isn't always working for me

replies.author: feexthefox
replies.body:
It's possible to put this as a skill, but you know, LLM have their limitations still, they're not magical 😛 

But i think its worth to try to do something like this, a "performance enhancer" for the code would be great

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body:
What do you mean by “operating closer to the engine”? Are you providing it the engine api or headers?

The thing I’ve found LLMs are very bad with (especially with game engines) is when there is a unique or custom abstraction that may actually be sound software engineering and architectural design but it doesn’t have training data on it.

I’ve found it quite bad at basic Godot development mostly because it makes a lot of assumptions about how it should work but it doesn’t work that way.

I’ve been thinking that maybe even just giving it access to the entire engine code base as context would help. But, that’s a pretty large context window to carry around.

This is why I ended up going back to nuts and bolts and am just working in plain C with really basic structs and a super simple architecture. But, I’m still interested in how we can get it working better with Godot.

replies.body: I tried asking ChatGPT to make me an AGENTS file for a 2d godot 4.5 game and with the best godot practices and it gave me text for the file after browsing the godot documentation. Earlier this year I created [Godot Runtime Bridge](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/4814) which gives Cursor/Codex the ability to build, test and debug with no need to touch the editor at all. So I just build by prompting now.

replies.author: feexthefox
replies.body:
That’s really cool, I’d love to take a look at your project!

That’s actually close to the direction I want to push this in: making Godot feel less intimidating, especially for beginners. Right now it’s still early, so the experience is not as smooth as I want yet. But the goal is to get to a point where you can explain what you want, and the tool can guide you, fix issues, test things, and handle a lot of the annoying editor friction for you

The tutorial side is a big part of that. I don’t want it to just generate code. I want it to help people understand what’s happening inside Godot while they build

comments.author: JTwoXX
comments.body:
Working on something similar in my spare time, l’ll definitely try this over the weekend!

Software as a harness seems like the obvious solution for tools. The trick I’ve found is to use a 2 tier agent approach. You’ll want an agent/model pairing specifically for capturing the users intent, and translating that into tool calls and actions within Godot. It should then pass that translation layer over to an orchestration agent/model pairing to handle the actual work.

Not saying the approach I took is law, but it’s what got me the best results thus far. The real issue at hand for me now is collecting and refining enough sample data for the translation layer to parse user intent properly. It seems maintaining a large vectorized database of genres and Godot functions related to them, is the most viable solution: outside of fine tuning a model specifically to act as the translation layer.

Exited to see your approach to this!
